strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: cross-domain generalization and adaptation of end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models, without resorting to costly LLM/MLLM retraining.

The proposed GP-based codebook formulation is a reasonably novel instantiation for this setting -- using basis tokens with matching trajectories to perform a Nadaraya-Watson/GP-style probabilistic 'lookup' provides a principled uncertainty estimate that is then used in three complementary ways (training regularization, adaptation supervision via pseudo-labels, and active-learning sample selection), which is a nice unification of ideas under one framework.

The experimental evaluation is fairly extensive: results are reported on standard nuScenes benchmark with a standardized evaluation protocol, cross-city transfer (Boston/Singapore), robustness to synthetic image corruptions (low light, motion blur), active learning under different sampling budgets, long-tail scenario evaluation, and comparison to a VLM-based baseline (VLP). This breadth of experiments strengthens the significance claims.

Consistent, non-trivial performance gains are reported across nearly all settings and metrics (e.g., collision rate reductions of 36-54% using the GP-based trajectory prediction, better zero-shot cross-city performance, better active-learning sample efficiency), applied to two different base models (VAD-T and SparseDrive-S), suggesting some generality of the approach.

Ablations (Table 6) isolate contributions of the reconstruction loss, classification loss, and triplet loss terms, and computational overhead is explicitly quantified (Table 5), which aids transparency about trade-offs.
The paper is generally clearly written with a reasonably detailed method description and an algorithm box/appendix that aids reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: The core claim of 'robust cross-domain' generalization is only validated on a single dataset (nuScenes) split by two cities (Boston/Singapore) plus synthetic corruptions; this is a narrow notion of 'domain' compared to the paper's motivating examples (different datasets, weather, sensor setups). No evaluation on a genuinely different dataset (e.g., Waymo, CARLA) is presented despite the introduction motivating broader domain shift.

The method depends on several design choices/hyperparameters (Ncode, C=64, group sizes 48/64, clustering of trajectories into groups from source-domain human driving data) whose sensitivity is not studied; it's unclear how brittle performance is to these choices or how they would be set for a genuinely new domain/base model.

The reconstruction/trajectory group classification (ce, ca) is itself a discrete, hard classification step (argmax into one of Ncode groups) prior to GP inference within that group; this seems to undermine the 'full' joint GP formulation advertised, and no ablation examines the impact of misclassification errors on downstream trajectory quality, especially in cross-domain settings where token distributions shift.

The comparison with VLP (Section D) uses a different (VAD) protocol because VLP's code isn't available, weakening the reliability of this cross-method comparison; similarly no comparison is provided against other cross-domain trajectory-prediction baselines mentioned in related work (Loh et al., Wang et al., AdapTraj, Ye et al.) despite an extensive related-work discussion of them.

Statistical significance/variance across runs is not reported anywhere (no error bars, no multiple seeds), which is a concern given some improvements (e.g., L2 differences of 0.01-0.05m) are numerically small relative to likely run-to-run variance.

The 'unsupervised domain adaptation' setting uses RoCA's own pseudo-labels (Lgp) as the sole adaptation signal, which risks confirmation bias/error accumulation if the GP's basis codebook is itself miscalibrated in the new domain; the paper does not analyze failure cases or provide any safeguard/discussion of when this self-training could degrade performance.

The extra inference-time GP module (used for the best reported numbers in Table 1) incurs non-trivial latency overhead (e.g., SparseDrive-S IPS drops from 7.5 to 6, ~25% latency increase), yet the abstract states the method improves generalizability 'without requiring extra inference computation,' which is only true for the training-regularization-only variant and could be seen as an overstated/ambiguous claim in the abstract given the strongest results require the costlier GP inference mode.

Qualitative results (Figs 3-5) are cherry-picked success cases; no failure-case analysis or discussion of the method's limitations (e.g., when basis coverage is insufficient, extreme domain shifts beyond two cities, rare classes not covered by clustered basis groups) is provided.

Reproducibility could be improved: no code release is mentioned, and some architectural/hyperparameter details (e.g., exact kernel bandwidth, MLP architecture for classification, choice of triplet positives/negatives selection procedure) are not fully specified in the main text.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underexplored problem: cross-domain generalization and adaptation for end-to-end autonomous driving without relying on costly LLM retraining.

The GP-based basis token/codebook formulation is a reasonably novel way to inject structured uncertainty into an E2E planner, and the idea of using GP predictive variance for both loss weighting and active-learning sample selection is appealing and coherently integrated into one framework.

Extensive experiments are provided across multiple axes: standard nuScenes evaluation, cross-city transfer (Boston/Singapore), active learning, image degradation robustness, long-tail scenario evaluation, and comparison with VLP, along with qualitative visualizations and a computation/latency analysis.
Consistent improvements over two different base models (VAD-T and SparseDrive-S) across nearly all reported metrics and settings suggest the method is not overfit to a single architecture.
Reasonable reproducibility details are given (training schedule, hardware, pseudocode in Algorithm 1, licensing info for datasets/models).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (nuScenes) and only two cities (Boston/Singapore), which are both US/Asia urban settings with relatively similar driving conventions aside from left/right-hand traffic; this is a narrow test of "cross-domain" generalization relative to the broad claims made (different cities, weather, camera characteristics, lighting). Weather/camera-characteristic generalization is only tested via synthetic corruptions (low light, motion blur) rather than real domain shift data.

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix, despite many close performance gaps (e.g., Table 1 differences of 0.01-0.02 m L2), making it hard to assess whether improvements are robust or within noise.

The GP formulation reuses a fairly standard GP regression/conditioning setup (Eqs. 1-4) applied per discrete anchor group; the technical novelty largely lies in combining existing components (anchor classification, GP posterior mean/variance, triplet loss, KL regularization) rather than a fundamentally new probabilistic model. The related-work section itself lists several prior GP-for-domain-adaptation papers, and the paper does not clearly differentiate its GP formulation from kernel-based nonparametric baselines (e.g., simple nearest-neighbor or kernel regression over basis trajectories) that could achieve similar effects without the full GP machinery.

The "RoCA trajectory prediction" mode, which gives the largest improvements in Table 1, requires running the GP module at inference time and incurs non-trivial extra latency/parameters (Table 5, e.g., +30% latency for SparseDrive-S), which somewhat undercuts the claimed "without requiring extra inference computation" advantage emphasized in the abstract; the abstract's generalizability claim without inference overhead applies only to the regularization-only variant, which shows smaller gains.

The number of basis groups (Nego=48, Nagent=64) and group size C=64 appear to be fixed design choices without ablation on sensitivity to these hyperparameters, nor justification for how trajectory clustering into these specific groups was performed or how robust results are to this choice.

Comparisons to recent LLM/VLM-based E2E driving approaches (which the introduction extensively motivates against) are largely qualitative discussion only; no direct quantitative comparison against any MLLM-based planner (e.g., only VLP, a non-LLM method, is compared in the appendix) is provided, despite the abstract and intro framing RoCA's advantage specifically relative to LLM-based methods.

The improvement magnitude in the most practically relevant and fair "same-domain" comparisons (Table 1, using ego status, RoCA training regularization only) is modest (0.65->0.63 m L2, 0.14->0.13% collision for SparseDrive-S), raising questions about the practical significance of the proposed regularization in well-matched domain settings.

The paper does not discuss failure cases, limitations of the proposed approach (e.g., scalability to much larger domain gaps, sensitivity to the quality/coverage of the clustering used to build the trajectory codebook, or when GP basis tokens fail to capture rare out-of-distribution behavior), nor any broader societal/safety discussion for a safety-critical application.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underexplored problem: cross-domain generalization and adaptation for end-to-end autonomous driving, without relying on expensive LLM retraining.

The proposed GP-based codebook formulation is a principled way to inject uncertainty estimation into E2E planning, and is model-agnostic (demonstrated on both VAD and SparseDrive), which increases its potential applicability.

The method provides multiple practical benefits in one framework: (1) a regularization effect that improves in-domain and cross-domain performance with no added inference cost, (2) an explicit trajectory-prediction mode with further gains at the cost of extra latency, (3) supervised and unsupervised adaptation, and (4) uncertainty-guided active learning for efficient data selection.

Experiments are extensive: standardized nuScenes evaluation protocol, cross-city transfer (Boston <-> Singapore), active learning at multiple sampling rates, robustness to image degradations (low light, motion blur), long-tail scenario evaluation, and a direct comparison to VLP under its original protocol. Ablations on loss terms are included.
Qualitative analyses (t-SNE of token clusters, example trajectories in challenging scenes) provide intuitive support for the claimed mechanism of improved separability/robustness.
Reasonable reproducibility details are given in the appendix (training schedule, hardware, pseudocode, latency/parameter counts), and licensing of datasets/baselines is disclosed.
weaknesses: The core technical formulation conflates a true Gaussian Process over functions with what appears to be a fixed, discrete, nearest-neighbor-style kernel regression over a small, hand-partitioned codebook (112 groups x 64 tokens); it is unclear how the hyperparameters of this "GP" (e.g., group count, size, kernel bandwidth) were chosen or how sensitive performance is to them, and no ablation over codebook size/group number is given.

The classification of tokens into a single hard group index (c_e, c_a) before applying GP regression breaks the probabilistic coherence of a joint GP formulation (mixing hard discrete classification with soft Bayesian inference) and is not clearly justified mathematically; the interaction between the classification loss, triplet loss, and the GP regression loss is complex and not analyzed in isolation beyond a coarse ablation.

Only two base models (VAD-T, SparseDrive-S) and one dataset (nuScenes, Boston/Singapore split) are used for all cross-domain experiments; generalization claims about "different cities, lighting, camera characteristics, weather" are only partially substantiated (only two cities, and only synthetic corruptions for lighting/blur, not real weather or camera-characteristic domain shifts).
The paper lacks closed-loop evaluation (e.g., CARLA or other simulators), which is a known limitation of open-loop L2/collision metrics for driving policies; this is not discussed as a limitation.

Added inference latency and parameter overhead when using the GP trajectory-prediction mode (Table 5) is non-trivial (e.g., +27% latency for SparseDrive-S) but this trade-off is understated in the main text relative to the performance gains claimed.

No explicit limitations section or discussion of failure cases, safety implications of relying on a fixed codebook of "safe" trajectories (e.g., what happens to truly novel maneuvers not covered by the human-driving-derived codebook, or adversarial/safety-critical rare events beyond the examined long-tail categories) is provided.

Statistical significance (e.g., variance across seeds, confidence intervals) is not reported for any of the main results tables, making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements (often modest, e.g., 0.63 vs 0.65 L2) are robust to run-to-run variation.

The comparison with VLP uses a different evaluation protocol (non-standardized) due to lack of released code, which weakens the strength of this specific comparison despite being transparently disclosed.

strengths: Extremely broad and thorough experimental evaluation, spanning closed-loop (Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, DriveArena) and open-loop (nuScenes) settings, four different base E2E architectures (VAD, SSR, SparseDrive, ORION), and multiple distinct domain-shift scenarios (sim-to-real, cross-city, image degradations, long-tail events).

Consistent and often substantial improvements over strong baselines across essentially all settings and base models, including improvements over LLM/VLM-based methods (ORION, DiMA, Senna) that are typically assumed to have superior world knowledge.

The method is practically attractive: when used purely as a training regularizer, RoCA improves in-domain and cross-domain performance with zero extra inference-time cost, since the GP module is discarded at deployment.

The uncertainty estimate from the GP formulation is put to good, well-motivated use beyond regularization -- it drives an effective active-learning sampling strategy that is compared favorably against MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles (Table 8), and supports label-free (unsupervised) adaptation that often outperforms supervised direct finetuning.

Extensive ablation studies in the appendix (loss term contributions, kernel choice, codebook size, comparison to deterministic/diffusion/VAE planner heads, motion-prediction metrics) support the design choices and provide useful robustness checks.
t-SNE visualizations and variance analyses offer some qualitative insight into why the method improves generalization (better-separated, semantically organized token clusters).
weaknesses: The claimed 'Gaussian Process' formulation is somewhat non-standard: standard GP regression typically involves optimizing kernel hyperparameters via log marginal likelihood, but here the 'GP' posterior mean/variance equations (Eqs. 3, 5) are applied over discrete, K-means-clustered basis groups with an RBF kernel and heuristic reconstruction/supervision losses, which is closer to a learned prototype/kernel-regression scheme dressed in GP notation than a fully Bayesian treatment; the paper does not clearly justify or verify the probabilistic calibration of the reported variances.

The overall training pipeline is multi-stage and fairly complex (pretrain base model, train basis tokens/GP, finetune with GP regularization, then adapt), which raises reproducibility concerns; no explicit statement about code/model release is given despite the many hyperparameters (Ncode, C, D, clustering procedure for basis trajectories) that would need to be fixed to reproduce results.

All reported numbers appear to be single-run point estimates with no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes small) improvements, especially in ablation tables (e.g., Table 11-13) where differences are marginal.

The characterization of 'unsupervised adaptation' is somewhat loose: the GP teacher module used to generate pseudo-labels during target-domain adaptation is itself trained with ground-truth supervision in the source domain, so the adaptation is better described as teacher-distillation from a source-supervised model rather than adaptation with no supervision signal anywhere in the pipeline; this framing could be clarified.

The main text is dense with many contributions and results, pushing crucial methodological details (e.g., training algorithm pseudocode, computation/latency analysis, full ablations) entirely into the appendix, which somewhat hampers self-contained readability of the core method.

The basis-token clustering procedure (sampling Ncode·C representative trajectories from ground-truth train data and clustering them) is described only briefly, leaving open questions about sensitivity to clustering algorithm/quality and how well this scales or generalizes to datasets with very different trajectory distributions than nuScenes/Bench2Drive.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underexplored problem: cross-domain generalization and efficient adaptation for end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving, without relying on costly LLM retraining.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning closed-loop (Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, DriveArena) and open-loop (nuScenes) settings, multiple base planners (VAD, SSR, SparseDrive, ORION), sim-to-real transfer, cross-city transfer, image degradations, active learning, and long-tail scenarios, showing generally consistent improvements.

The idea of using GP predictive variance to guide active-learning sample selection and to serve as a 'teacher' signal for unsupervised adaptation is a reasonable and practically useful extension beyond standard fine-tuning.

Reasonably thorough ablations in the appendix (loss components, kernel choice, codebook size, comparison to MC-Dropout/Deep Ensembles, comparison to deterministic/diffusion/VAE planner heads) that attempt to isolate sources of improvement.
The method is presented as plug-and-play and architecture-agnostic, requiring only tokenized ego/agent representations, which could ease adoption across different E2E stacks.
weaknesses: The core GP formulation is not a genuine joint Gaussian process over the full codebook; tokens are first hard-classified into a single basis group via an MLP-on-kernel-distance, and the GP machinery is only applied within that small group. This undermines the claimed 'probabilistic joint distribution over tokens' narrative and makes the method closer to a soft nearest-group regression/reconstruction scheme dressed in GP notation. The self-covariance term κ(e) used in the variance formulas is not carefully defined (for common kernels like RBF this is a constant), raising doubts about whether the reported 'uncertainty' is meaningfully calibrated rather than a byproduct of distance-to-basis-mean.

No code, trained models, or basis-token initialization/clustering procedure are released or fully specified (e.g., exact clustering algorithm for forming trajectory groups, sensitivity to cluster quality), which limits reproducibility given the many moving parts (codebook sizes, group counts, multi-stage training schedule, stop-gradient treatment of e/a).

The motivation explicitly argues against LLM-based approaches due to retraining cost and lack of generalization guarantees, yet the strongest reported numbers are obtained by applying RoCA on top of ORION, itself a vision-language-instructed (LLM-based) planner — this is in tension with the paper's stated positioning and makes it unclear how much of the gain is attributable to RoCA versus the LLM backbone.

The abstract claims the method improves generalizability 'without requiring extra inference computation,' but Appendix A.4 shows that the better-performing 'trajectory prediction' mode of RoCA increases latency by ~25-30% and adds parameters; the claim only holds for the weaker 'training regularization only' variant, which is a non-trivial caveat not reflected in the abstract/intro framing.

Many reported gains are very large relative to baselines (e.g., halved collision rates, large driving-score jumps) without any variance/error bars, multiple-seed reporting, or statistical significance testing, which is concerning given the complexity of the multi-stage training pipeline (pretrain → learn basis/GP → regularized fine-tune → adapt) and the number of hyperparameters (Ncode, C, D, noise variance, triplet margins) that could be tuned per experiment.

Baseline reproduction fidelity is unclear: several comparison numbers (e.g., DriveTransformer-L, ORION, GenAD, Senna, DiMA) appear to be taken from original papers under potentially different training budgets/configurations rather than reproduced under identical conditions, making head-to-head comparisons in Tables 1-3 less reliable.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations/discussion section analyzing failure cases, scenarios where the basis-token codebook might fail to generalize (e.g., truly novel maneuvers not represented by any cluster), or the sensitivity of the hard group-classification step to misclassification errors.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation spanning closed-loop (Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, DriveArena) and open-loop (nuScenes) settings, multiple base planners (VAD, SSR, SparseDrive, ORION), cross-city transfer, sim-to-real transfer, image degradation robustness, active learning, and long-tail scenario analysis — this breadth of validation is unusually comprehensive for a single paper.

The method is genuinely plug-and-play: it is shown to improve several different recent E2E architectures (including an LLM-based planner, ORION) without modifying their core architecture, and the improvements are consistent and often substantial (e.g., driving score, collision rate, L2 error) across nearly every table.

The idea of using a GP over a learned codebook of basis tokens to provide both (1) a regularizing teacher signal during source training and (2) an uncertainty estimate usable for active learning and unsupervised adaptation is a reasonably novel combination applied to the specific problem of cross-domain E2E driving, which the authors argue (with supporting citations) is underexplored.

Useful ablations in the appendix (loss components, kernel choice, codebook size, comparison to MC-Dropout/Deep Ensembles and alternative generative planner heads) that help isolate the contribution of individual design choices.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (training time, GPU count, epoch counts, pseudocode algorithms, hyperparameters for the codebook) is provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The GP formulation is non-standard in a way that is not fully justified theoretically: ego/agent tokens are first hard-classified into one of Ncode discrete groups (via an MLP over kernel distances) before GP conditioning is applied only within that group. This conflates a discrete nearest-group lookup with a continuous GP posterior, and the paper does not discuss how gradients propagate through this argmax-like classification step, raising questions about optimization stability and whether the claimed 'joint probabilistic distribution over all tokens' is actually realized.

In the reconstruction/basis-learning stage, the original ego/agent tokens e, a from the base model are treated as frozen targets ('no gradients flow through them'), meaning the codebook is fit to approximate a source-domain-frozen feature space; this could limit how well the probabilistic structure actually captures target-domain variation, yet the paper claims strong unsupervised target adaptation without clearly reconciling this tension.

All reported numbers appear to be single-run point estimates; there are no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or multiple-seed results anywhere in the main paper or appendix, which is a concern given how many fine-grained comparisons (e.g., 0.01–0.05 differences in L2/collision rate) are used to support claims of superiority.

The abstract/intro claims RoCA improves the base model 'without requiring extra inference computation,' but Table 10 (appendix) shows the GP-based trajectory-prediction mode increases latency by ~20-30% and adds parameters; the paper should more clearly delineate when the 'no extra inference cost' claim holds (training-regularization-only mode) versus when it does not (GP-as-predictor mode), since several headline results (e.g., Tables 1, 2) appear to use RoCA as part of inference.

Reproducibility is only partial: no code or model release is mentioned, several baselines (ORION, DiMA, Senna) are reported via re-implementation/re-training without discussion of whether official checkpoints or hyperparameters were matched, which raises fairness concerns for the numerous head-to-head comparisons.

The construction of the trajectory codebook relies on offline clustering of ground-truth trajectories into Ncode groups; the sensitivity of results to clustering algorithm/quality (beyond just group count) is not analyzed, and it's unclear how this step would generalize to domains with very different trajectory distributions (e.g., different traffic rules) without manual re-clustering.

While the method is described as supporting 'online adaptation,' no experiment actually demonstrates or quantifies online/streaming adaptation performance (e.g., latency-accuracy tradeoff over a driving sequence); this contribution claim in the introduction is not empirically substantiated in the body of the paper.

Figures 3/4 (t-SNE separability) are presented as evidence that RoCA produces better-structured embeddings, but t-SNE visualizations are qualitative and depend on hyperparameters; no quantitative clustering metric (e.g., silhouette score) is reported to substantiate the claim of improved separability.
